newsitem.title: UK: Treasuries stay firm in London ahead of ECI.
newsitem.headline: Treasuries stay firm in London ahead of ECI.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries were steady at higher levels in London trade on Tuesday as the market bet on a relatively benign employment cost index later, analysts said.
They said Treasuries still had scope to rally on a weak number, but added with so many investors going long into the figures, the balance of risk for the market was on the downside.

"Sentiment looks pretty positive at the moment," said Jeremy Hawkins, economic adviser at Bank America here. "A good ECI number is pretty much discounted...but as long as the year-on-year rate comes in below 3.0 percent, there's scope for the market to go a bit further."

By 0950 GMT, the 30-year cash bond was at 102-29 to yield 6.4 percent, from 102-28 in Tokyo and 102-29 at the New York close. The 10-year paper was at 103-18, unchanged from Tokyo and down from 103-19 in New York.
According to a Reuter poll, the second quarter ECI is expected to rise 0.8 percent on the quarter, after a 0.6 percent increase in the first quarter.
Hawkins said annual growth above 3.0 percent could spell trouble for the market.
"If we get 3.1 percent, it will wipe out yesterday's gains without too many problems," he said.
One dealer at a U.S. bank in London said the market was trying to push a bit higher, but said volume was fairly low.
"If we get a benign ECI number -- as long as the dollar holds versus the mark -- the September future could push up to 116," he said.
"But I think the balance of risk is on the downside."
By 1000 GMT, the September T-bond future was up 5/32 at 115-19 in automated trade.
He said investors were relatively long going into the data, but added if the opportunity arose, there was quite a lot of money on the sidelines ready to come in.
Analysts said a mild ECI number would set a positive tone for the rest of the week, culminating in payrolls data on Friday.
"If the ECI is OK, it's difficult to see anything coming out of the GDP accounts (on Thursday) that would be worrying," said Hawkins.
"In the back end of the week there may be worries about payrolls...but in the interim it looks like the numbers will be pretty supportive."
Hawkins said he would prefer to be in the long end of the curve going into the raft of data this week.
"People are starting to mark down their expectations about inflation, so the longer end is still attractive," he said.
"We could still get to 6.25 percent (long bond yield) if the numbers continue to behave themselves, particularly with a strong dollar."
Also due out on Tuesday was the consumer confidence index for July at 1400 GMT and the Redbook Retail Sales Index for the week ending July 26 at 1855 GMT.
-- Jennifer Scott, International Bonds Unit +44 171 542 8682
